content:
Yesterday saw two contradictory reports about next year's iPhone 20th anniversary edition, which is said to embody Apple's long-term vision of a "single slab of glass."

There have long been contradictory reports on what exactly we should expect, but yesterday's divergence was the biggest so far...

What we know so far

Former Apple design chief Jony Ive has frequently spoken of his long-term vision of the iPhone eventually becoming a single slab of glass. The company is generally believed to still be pursuing this vision after Ive's departure.

Although Apple generally doesn't make a big deal of various anniversaries of its products, the prevailing view is that the company aims to get as close as possible to this vision with the iPhone's 20th anniversary. This could include embedding Face ID under the display, with the front camera also potentially hidden beneath the screen.

However, as to what exactly we can expect, we've already seen contradictory reports. Some initially thought it would be a standalone model similar to the iPhone Air and the upcoming iPhone Ultra, but more recent reports have pointed to this design being applied to next year's iPhone Pro models.

In order, this would be the iPhone 19 Pro, but Apple may also want to skip this name and jump straight to iPhone 20 to mark the anniversary.

Yesterday's contradictory reports

Things got even more confusing yesterday, when an analyst claimed Apple had abandoned plans for an all-glass iPhone next year.

However, Bloomberg's Mark Gurman quickly came out to refute this claim.

The most likely reality

The key point is that Apple's vision for the iPhone doesn't have a single endpoint. Whatever the company plans to launch next year will only be one or a few steps closer to that sci-fi vision of a "single slab of glass."

The question isn't whether this goal will be achieved next year, but how far the company will advance toward that vision. But whether it's one step or several, it certainly won't be the last step in the evolution of iPhone design.

In fact, Gurman says Apple has stepped back from the goal it had originally hoped to achieve next year.

It's quite possible that the Jefferies analyst heard the same news, but only heard it more recently and interpreted it as a complete abandonment of the plan.

My own expectation is that next year's design will be a major leap—on par with the introduction of the iPhone X—but there will be further developments over the coming years. For me, the biggest question is whether the 2027 iPhone will have enough breakthroughs to warrant Apple giving it a special branding, whether it's labelled as the 20th anniversary edition iPhone (which I think is unlikely), given another special name, or skips a generation to be called iPhone 20.

What are your expectations? Feel free to share your thoughts in the comments.
